title: MB9-16246
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Nigeria and the General Overseer of the Power of Faith Pentecostal International Church in Nigeria. The Appellant fears persecution as he is wanted by the governors of the states of Kaduna, Oyo and Benue.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) did not find the Appellant's claim or testimony credible. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred due to its complete lack of analysis of his request for protection and his supporting documentation and in its assessment of his credibility.
Following my own review, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant did not credibly establish his claim.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing and weighing the oral testimony heard, which in particular cases attracts deference.1 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied the correctness standard.
The determinative issue is credibility.
The RPD identified several credibility issues and concluded that it did not believe the allegations at the heart of the Appellant's claim and did not find his testimony to be trustworthy.

The Appellant submits that the RPD's decision is "entachÕe et doit etre annulÕe" due to its complete lack of analysis of his request for protection and his supporting documentation and its erroneous assessment of his credibility based on alleged contradictions. Analysis of credibility in refugee claims

The process of determining whether a claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) requires the RPD to decide whether they believe the claimant's evidence and how much weight to give that evidence. In determining this the RPD must assess the credibility of the claimant and the documentary evidence.2 The law "imposes a duty upon RPD members to assess the credibility of refugee claimants."3

The Federal Court4 has laid out the relevant principles in analyzing credibility in the context of refugee claims: * Refugee applicants are presumed to tell the truth, but this is a presumption rebuttable by the applicant's lack of credibility, e.g. where the evidence is inconsistent with sworn testimony or where the applicant's explanation for the inconsistencies is not satisfactory; * Even though they may be insufficient when taken individually or in isolation, the accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies and omissions regarding crucial elements of a refugee claim can support a negative conclusion about an applicant's credibility; * A negative credibility finding cannot be based on minor contradictions that are secondary or peripheral to the refugee protection claim; * A lack of credibility concerning central elements of a refugee protection claim can extend and trickle down to other elements of the claim and be generalized to all of the documentary evidence presented to corroborate a version of the facts; * Credibility findings should not be made based strictly on the absence of corroborative evidence. Where corroborative evidence should reasonably be available to establish an essential element of a claim and there is no reasonable explanation for its absence, a decision-maker can draw a negative inference of credibility based on the claimant's lack of effort to obtain such corroborative evidence; and * Conclusions can be drawn concerning an applicant's credibility based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality.

I have reviewed the evidence on the record, the testimony and arguments of the Appellant. For the reasons outlined below, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's claim is not credible due to omissions, inconsistencies and contradictions in his evidence about central elements of his claim and behaviour incompatible with a fear of persecution.

I find that the RPD did make some errors, specifically its decision does not reflect that it considered the Appellant's supporting documentation. The error is not determinative because, as detailed below I have reviewed all the documents presented to the RPD. I find that the Appellant's documentary evidence does not overcome the negative credibility finding and that an absence of corroborative evidence, which should reasonably have been available, supports the negative credibility finding. RPD credibility findings

The RPD identified several credibility issues. The Appellant's failure to reference that he was wanted by the governors of the states of Kaduna, Oyo and Benue and his eight-month relocation to Apasan on his immigration form. A contradiction between the Appellant's testimony, immigration forms and passport with respect to trips to Italy in 2016. The Appellant's visit to Italy and return to Nigeria in XXXX 2016 and his delay in waiting to leave Nigeria until XXXX 2017 was behaviour inconsistent with someone fearing for his safety.

The Appellant submits the RPD decision did not assess the merits of his claim and focused on superficial contradictions rather than assessing the facts and his risks of persecution. The Appellant cites the recent Supreme Court of Canada to support his arguments that the RPD decision was a "failure to meaningfully grapple with key issues or central arguments raised by the parties may call into question whether the decision maker was actually alert and sensitive to the matter before it"5

The Appellant argues that the RPD did not make any findings about important parts of his story or identify any contradictions in his testimony, or between his BOC and testimony. I do not agree and, find, as detailed below that each of the credibility issues identified by the RPD go to the heart of the Appellant's claim. Appellant's evidence about being wanted by Nigerian authorities

The Appellant's evidence about being wanted by Nigerian authorities is not consistent: BOC narrative6 Testimony Immigration form7 Other Governor of Kaduna State demanded the Appellant's arrest "dead or alive" and contacted Governors in Oyo and Benue State to influence his arrest anywhere RPD: Who do you fear exactly in Nigeria? Appellant: It was the government of Kaduna... RPD: So you fear the governor of Kaduna? Appellant: Yes...8 RPD: Do you know if there's a warrant for your arrest in Nigeria? Do you know if they officially want to arrest you? If there's a warrant for your arrest? Appellant: I don't know because I hide myself. They don't know where I am. I cannot come out. RPD: Did you try to find out? Appellant: I did not try to find out.9 RPD: As you mentioned the governor was looking for you. How did you find out about that? Appellant: Through radio.10 Appellant did not indicate that he was wanted by Nigerian authorities "I can confirm that the [Appellant] had been accused of causing religious Problem which has leads to government of Kaduna and Oyo State hunting for his life in Nigeria...I confirm his family has be on the monitoring list of government since 2016."11 "...[the Appellant] was leaving a miserable life moving from house to villages in order to escape from the Kaduna government hunting for his life."12

When the RPD asked the Appellant why he had not stated that he was being sought by Nigerian authorities on his immigration form he said that he "did not go to police station, police did not catch me."13 The RPD did not find the explanation satisfactory because the fact that the Appellant is being sought by Nigerian authorities is the basis of his refugee protection claim. The RPD found that the Appellant's failure to answer the clear question on the immigration form, "have you ever been sought, arrested, or detained by the police or military or any other authorities in any country, including Canada?" constituted a significant omission.

The Appellant argues that he misunderstood the question on the immigration form; he signed the immigration form on January 12, 2018 but the details were clearly laid out in his BOC signed on January 29, 2018. His evidence on the subject is direct and detailed and he explained the omission in a reasonable manner because he was not arrested in Nigeria but was arrested at the Canadian border so he only listed that arrest on the form.

I agree with the RPD that the omission is material because it goes to the heart of the Appellant's claim and I cannot agree with the Appellant, as detailed in the table above, that his evidence about being sought by the Nigerian authorities is direct and detailed. The Appellant's evidence is inconsistent on its face about: who is looking for him (three governors or just one or two); whether an arrest warrant was in fact issued and by whom; and which government has him on a monitoring list. Appellant's evidence about his location from October 2016 - July 2017

The Appellant's evidence about where he was living from October 2016- July 2017 is not consistent: BOC narrative14 Testimony Immigration form15 Other "Since [October 2016] my church had been placed on surveillance and had I been hidden around here and there fighting for my life... I was in a farm in a village named "Apasan" hidden here and there for my life safety until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017" RPD: Apasan. Ok. So you were there for 6 months...So you were there from when to when exactly? Appellant: I was there, I got there on XXXX XXXX XXXX RPD: Which year? Appellant: 2016. RPD: Until? Appellant: I left there around the XXXX XXXX XXXX...I was staying with an elderly woman, she farms there.16 XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Arimasahun Street, Ibadan Nigeria XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Arimasahun Street, Ibadan Nigeria XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Montoval Italy "...we did not know the where about of the [the Appellant] and his family in 2016...we couldn't find him and his family until recently we learnt that the [Appellant] is in United States later in Canada... [the Appellant] was leaving a miserable life moving from house to villages in order to escape from the Kaduna government hunting for his life."17

When the RPD asked the Appellant why he failed to mention his eight-month relocation to Apasan on his immigration form he explained that when he completed the form, he understood that he had to provide his addresses for the past 10 years. He thought that he had to provide the street number and name and, since Apasan is a village, he did not have that information.18

The RPD found the Appellant's explanation unsatisfactory because his allegation that he was living in hiding in Apasan for the eight months following the October 22, 2016 events, out of fear that the governors of the states of Kaduna, Oyo and Benue would find him, goes to the heart of his claim for protection. The RPD noted that question 12 on form IMM566919 asked the Appellant to list all the addresses where he lived in the past 10 years and he listed more than 12 addresses. In the circumstances, the RPD found it is reasonable to expect the Appellant to have included the various addresses where he sought refuge for eight months. The RPD also notes that, at question 8 of the same form, the Appellant stated that he worked with the XXXX in Ibadan until December 2016.

The Appellant argues that his explanation was reasonable and that he gave street names and numbers for all the places he listed. I note that this is not accurate as the Appellant did not give a street address for either of the two visits to Italy listing "Christ Evangelical In Montoval In Italy" on the form.20

The Appellant also argues that his BOC, which was filed a few days later, clarified his mistake. The Appellant submits that the omission relates to a peripheral element of his claim and that his evidence is clear and without contradiction. I do not agree.

I find that the omission is material because it goes to the heart of the Appellant's claim as he was hiding in Apasan because he feared persecution. I also cannot agree with the Appellant, as detailed in the table above, that his evidence about where he stayed from October 2016 to July 2017 is without contradiction. The Appellant's evidence is inconsistent on its face about when he went to Apasan (on XXXX XXXX or after moving house to house village to village) and when he left (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Appellant's trip to Italy

The Appellant's evidence about his trips to Italy was also inconsistent: Immigration form21 Passport Testimony XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Christ Evangelical In Montoval In Italy XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Christ Evangelical In Montoval In Italy Schengen Visa valid from 09-06-16 to 03-07-1622 Schengen Visa valid from 23-11-16 to 07-01-1623 Lagos exit stamp XXXX XXXX 201624 Malpensa entry stamp XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX25 Malpensa exit stamp XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX26 Lagos entry stamp XXXX XXXX XXXX27 RPD: How many times did you go to Italy? Appellant: Once. RPD: Once? When was that? Appellant: June. RPD: And how long did you stay there? Appellant: One week.28 RPD: But I don't understand why [at question 8 on form IMM5669] it is indicated that you went to Italy in November-December 2016. Appellant: Because the stamp is on my passport. That's why I indicated that, that I travelled. RPD: The stamp is on your passport but you didn't go? Appellant: I didn't go.29

The RPD asked the Appellant to explain the contradiction between his immigration form, passport and his testimony regarding the trip to Italy in XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016. The Appellant testified that the individual who had helped him organize his departure from Nigeria had his passport stamped to indicate he had travelled to Italy in November "[b]ecause there is a visa in that passport. That maybe they would ask me questions at why have not used it, the visa."30

The RPD also asked the Appellant to explain why, at question 8 of form IMM5669, he had stated that he had travelled to Italy in XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016 after the incident on October 16, 2016 that had caused him to fear for his life in Nigeria. The Appellant explained that he had done so in order for the information in his immigration forms to be consistent with the information in his passport.31

The RPD found that the Appellant's explanation was not reasonable. Had the Appellant, in fact, not travelled to Italy two weeks after the incident that he claims put his life in danger in Nigeria, it is reasonable to expect that he would not have indicated that he travelled to Italy in XXXX 2016 in response to question 8 of form IMM5669.
The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony was not credible and that he went to Italy in XXXX 2016 and returned to Nigeria in XXXX 2016.
The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by not considering the clear and convincing explanation provided by the Appellant. I do not agree.

Based on the Schengen visa, the stamps in the Appellant's passport, the immigration forms and the unreasonableness of his explanation I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did visit Italy in XXXX XXXX XXXX2016. This finding undermines the Appellant's truthfulness about other aspects of his claim and reinforces the RPD's negative credibility findings about whether the Appellant was wanted by the Nigerian authorities and spent eight months in hiding in Apasan. Behaviour incompatible with fear of persecution

In addition to the Appellant's trip to Italy and return to Nigeria, the RPD identified other behaviours which raised credibility concerns. The RPD asked the Appellant why he waited until XXXX 2017 to leave Nigeria when he had a valid visa for the United States since XXXX 2016 given his testimony that he heard on the radio on October 22, 2016 that people were looking for him in order to kill him.32

The Appellant's first response that he did not leave because of the church program he wanted to complete33 then he said that he could not leave because he was in hiding he "cannot go out to any transaction maybe to buy ticket or to go anywhere."34 The explanations are, on their face, contradictory. The Appellant, ignoring the contradiction, argues that his explanation that he was in hiding and that he could not procure a ticket is reasonable.

I agree with the RPD that, if the Appellant truly feared for his life, he would not have left Nigeria for Italy in XXXX 2016 and then returned to Nigeria in XXXX 2016 nor would he have waited eight months to leave Nigeria when he had a valid visa for the United States. Corroborative evidence

The RPD concluded that it did believe the Appellant or that he was threatened or bothered in any way, by any authorities in Nigeria, because of his religious activities with the "Power of Faith Pentecostal International Church". The RPD stated that it did not believe the Appellant's account as a whole and attached no probative value to the documents submitted as evidence in support of his allegations.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by rejecting all of his documentary proof as having no probative value without having considered it. I agree and have considered the corroborative evidence of the Appellant.

As detailed above in paragraphs 14 and 18, I have found that the evidence in the two affidavits35 from the Appellant's church members was inconsistent with his BOC and testimony and so accord them little evidentiary weight.

I have reviewed all the documentation36 presented about the Appellant's church and find that it does not corroborate the material elements of his claim with respect to the events in October 2016. I find that the photographs of the sealed church and burnt house and church37 are not labelled with the location of the properties, dated or authenticated and so do not have probative value as evidence to corroborate the Appellant's claim.

I also find that the absence of corroborative evidence which should reasonably have been available supports the negative credibility findings of the RDP. The Appellant states, "[l]es mÕdias locaux rapportaient l'assassinat de plus de 25 personnes lors de cette attaque perpÕtrÕe contre l'èglise; au moins 70 blessÕs Õtaient Õgalement recensÕs".38 When the RPD questioned the Appellant about why he did not provide copies of the newspaper articles about the October 16, 2016 bomb attack, he responded that he did not have access to Nigeria and he cannot send newspapers from Nigeria. When the RPD asked why the two church members who provided affidavits did not send the newspaper articles, he said he could not ask them to send the newspapers because he did not have an address.39 I find that the Appellant did not provide a reasonable explanation for the absence of newspaper articles and I draw a negative inference of credibility based on his lack of effort to obtain such corroborative evidence.

I have also reviewed the objective evidence and note that there are no reports of a bomb attack in Kaduri in Kaduna State on October 16, 2016 by Muslim fanatics as described by the Appellant in his RPD testimony resulting in a burnt church, car and neighbouring houses, 25 deaths and 70 injuries.40 There are, however, other reports about events in Kaduna State in October 2016 specifically that the media reported gunmen believed to be Fulani herdsman who killed 40 people in Godoogodo, Kaduna State41 and that police in Kaduna banned the Islamic Movement in Nigeria (IMN) the country's largest Shiite organization and at least 11 people died during the annual Ashure processions.42 The Appellant submits that the evidence of these attacks support his claim.43 I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the attack alleged by the Appellant in October 2016, given the number of deaths and injuries and amount of destruction, would have been referenced in the objective evidence if it had occurred.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
